Here's how the three paths compare across the dimensions that matter most for your Series A goal.

Capital efficiency vs runway security
The Lean Path (£250k) preserves more equity and signals discipline to Series A investors, but gives you less buffer if growth slows. At 10% month-on-month from £18k MRR, you need roughly 17 months to hit £50k organically. Eight months of current runway plus £250k buys you time, but not much margin for error. The Growth Path (£750k) extends your runway significantly and lets you hire or spend into faster growth, but at the cost of more dilution now.

Dilution timing
Raising more now means giving up more equity at your current (lower) valuation. If you hit £50k MRR before Series A, your valuation will be materially higher. The Lean Path bets you can get there cheaply; the Growth Path bets that speed is worth the dilution cost.

Execution risk
The Status Quo path is the most revealing comparison: your organic trajectory suggests you could reach £50k MRR in roughly 17 months without raising, which is outside your 12-month window. That makes some raise almost certainly necessary. The real question is whether £250k is enough to close the gap, or whether £750k is needed to accelerate meaningfully.

The assumption doing the most work
Your model has no cost or budget factor. That means the analysis cannot yet distinguish between the two raise amounts in terms of what you'd actually spend the money on. Before running the numbers, the single most useful thing to add is: what does each raise amount let you do differently? More hires? More marketing spend? The most important gap right now is cost. Your model has no salary cost factor connected to the goal, which means the three options look identical on budget impact. At £85k per year and 18 months of runway, the difference between a £70k tech lead and two £45k juniors is material.

Beyond cost, two things shape this decision most:

Whether technical direction is already covered. Your team has one senior developer. If that person can provide architectural guidance for the rewrite, a tech lead adds less value and two juniors give you more delivery throughput. If the senior is stretched or not suited to that role, the tech lead path becomes much stronger.

Ramp-up time against your runway. Two junior developers typically take 3-6 months to reach full productivity. On an 18-month runway, that's a significant fraction. A tech lead usually ramps faster but contributes differently. The rewrite timeline is the pressure point.

The single most useful thing you can tell me: how well is your current senior developer covering technical direction? That one answer would most change which option the model favours.
